4f9462f9d5edcb98: Kemerdekaan Malaysia kini masuk ke gerbang angka 69 tahun. Tahun hadapan ia akan menjadi yang ke-70. Sebahagian dari tempoh itu, kita menikmatinya bersama-sama Sabah dan Sarawak.

Dalam tempoh mendewasa ini, jenama 'Malaysia' pernah berdepan ancaman komunisme, perkauman yang menumpahkan darah, tidak kurang juga ancaman dari negara jiran yang menanggapi kita dengan cara yang salah; ataupun menginginkan bahagian dari negara ini. Semua getir manis bersama-sama tersebut telah menjadikan kita matang.

Namun demikian, kematangan itu harus sentiasa dipupuk dan tidak boleh diabaikan. Silibus pendidikan misalnya mestilah seiring bergerak untuk mengasuh rakyat agar terus dapat maju ke hadapan, dan bukan berpatah balik membelakang. Hari ini ada suara-suara mahu mengkhianati jenama 'Malaysia' ini. Suara dan teriak yang makin keras itu mahu kembali ke era romantis iaitu jenama 'Tanah Melayu' yang dengan sendirinya mengikis hak-hak sedia ada kaum lain dan Sabah Sarawak yang telah ikut membina jenama 'Malaysia' di mata dunia.

Akan tetapi ancaman kemerdekaan negara kita -- meski masih sedikit sebanyak serupa isunya -- sedang berdepan dua gugatan yang ketara nyata. Kita tidak perlu pergi jauh untuk melihat risiko kecelakaan ini. Ia terbentang di hadapan mata. Bahkan sebetulnya, ia ada di tangan kita dan kadang-kala digerakkan oleh kita sendiri.

Ancaman kemerdekaan ini mestilah ditangani segera. Saya belum melihat kerja-kerja matang, dewasa dan bersungguh-sungguh dari mana pihak pun untuk memadamkan api kecelakaan yang perlahan-lahan merumba dan memarak. Ia boleh membakar hangus kita jika kita tidak berhati-hati.

Ancaman pertama adalah normalisasi rasuah. Ancaman rasuah ini semakin hari semakin kelihatan dan sudah mengental menjadi satu ideologi. Saya pernah menyatakan di kolum ini yang rasuahisme boleh menyaingi faham seperti nasionalisme, komunisme, feminisme, dan macam-macam lagi. Oleh sebab ia satu ideologi, ia kini mampu bersaing; ia boleh melekat, melekap, bersenyawa, beranak-pinak dan kemudian bermutasi, bergabung lantas mensebati dengan faham-faham sedia ada untuk membentuk satu ciri atau kriteria baru yang menakutkan.

Seperti alien yang tahan, rasuahisme ini boleh menyedut masuk nasionalisme, Islamisme, dan sekian isme lain lantas memberikan ia bentuk baharu yang lebih berbahaya, menakutkan, dan jauh lebih merosakkan.

Dalam keadaan itu rasuahisme dianggap normal. Ia dianggap sebahagian dari kehidupan dan hayat insan atau rakyat kita. Rasuahisme yang patut dibenci kini didambai. Berapa banyak ungkapan yang kita temukan, 'ingin kembali ke era sakau', 'sanggup hidup semula di zaman 1MDB', 'merindui Bapak Rasuah Dunia', dan rasuah disanjung sebagai majikan, sebagai bos, sebagai tok nenek, sebagai raja.

Dalam keadaan gejala inilah rasuahisme itu dipandang damai, didambai sebagai keindahan, dan dicipta-ciptakan oleh Kak Long betapa segala naratif palsu bagi membolehkan ia menjadi sesuatu yang normal. Apabila ia terpandang normal, ia akan menjadi sesuatu yang mudah meresap dalam segenap pembuluh darah harian kita.

Dalam kancah gejala inilah, perompakan secara kreatif Tabung Haji dipandang sebagai sesuatu yang tidak apa-apa. Hatta menyebutnya dalam grup WhatsApp keluarga, surau atau kejiranan akan dianggap sensitif atau taboo. Padahal ia adalah satu kuman jijik yang mesti dibincangkan. Mereka yang ingin menyuarai kebimbangan ini akan dimusuhi, dipertangkari dan dianggap elemen selingkuh. Padahal ia suara waras.

Dalam gejala normalisasi rasuahisme inilah perompakan Tabung Haji cuba disahkan dengan cara bertanya kembali, 'bukankah tiada kata sakau', atau dibikin forum konon ilmiah untuk mewajarkan perompakan, dan lebih dahsyat naratif penipuan diketengahkan dengan cara menyatakan ketika perompakan itu terjadi, 'tiada duit yang hilang kerana anda masih boleh mengeluarkan wang'.

Negara ini terancam bertukar kerajaan lagi menjelang pilihan raya umum. Penangguhan demi penangguhan akan pendakwaan dan perjalanan kes mahkamah untuk sang sakau terancam berisiko untuk dibubarkan kelak. Perhatikan sahaja dalam keadaan ini hanya agensi seperti Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia yang berdepan dengan segala kudrat tenaga ada untuk melawan dan menjadi benteng negara. Agensi penguatkuasa yang lain terus longlai lemau.

Rasuahisme dibaja dipugar kadang-kala oleh mereka yang sepatutnya matang. Pengkaji rasuahisme di negara kita, Syed Hussein Alatas mengatakan, "Dalam hal rasuah, penyumbang utama dalam penciptaan ideologi rasuah yang terselubung itu adalah sejumlah kecil wartawan dan beberapa orang profesor di perguruan tinggi. Mereka mungkin tidak sedar terhadap apa yang mereka lakukan, iaitu membantu dan mendorong amalan rasuah dengan menawarkan bahan-bahan untuk ideologi rasuah yang diperlukan oleh orang yang rasuah. Tulisan mereka mempunyai pengaruh yang mengecilkan erti pemerasan, ketidakadilan, dan kekejaman yang dilakukan terhadap bahagian terbesar umat manusia."

Tidaklah menghairankan kita melihat ada wartawan di wadah tertentu, khusus yang berkait parti, akan beria-ia mempertahankan rasuahisme. Profesor di universiti yang menanti dengan lahap gred lebih tinggi akan bersikeras membuktikan rasuahisme ini normal.
Maka dengan demikianlah ideologi celaka ini diturunkan kepada generasi baharu. Lihat sahaja bagaimana normalnya sesetengah Gen Z di media sosial memuji dan memuja gejala rasuahisme.

Ancaman kedua adalah ekstremisme agama. Sebagai visiting senior fellow di ISEAS-Yusof Ishak sejak tahun 2020, antara peranan saya adalah mengkaji gejala ekstremisme tanpa kekerasan (NVE) di mana ia adalah secara mudahnya pengungkapan fahaman politik, agama atau ideologi yang ekstrem tanpa menggunakan kekerasan fizikal, melakukan kerosakan harta benda atau melibatkan diri dalam keganasan.

Penyokong, pemuja dan penggerak NVE biasanya tidak menyedari mereka di dalam kancah kemelut kultus atau ajaran NVE. Acap kali mereka adalah kelompok profesional. Hanya apabila mereka terpancut keluar dari organisasi ekstrem ini barulah mereka melihat apa yang mereka gelumangi selama ini. Perspektif dari luar ini penting tetapi selalu dinafikan oleh mereka.

Kelompok ini akan berpegang dan mendakwahkan idea-idea radikal yang menolak nilai-nilai demokrasi arus perdana secara terang atau secara sembunyi; menolak keterangkuman sosial dengan memomokkan kaum tertentu atau kepercayaan tertentu, dan biasanya akan dianggap normal kerana tidak (atau belum) melibatkan penggunaan kekerasan fizikal secara langsung.

Meskipun ia dinamai ekstremisme tanpa kekerasan, ia masih bersumberkan ideologi asas yang sama dengan ekstremisme ganas, dan ia berjenama gerakan berhaluan kanan ekstrem, kiri ekstrem dan gerakan berasaskan agama. Siapa sahaja akan terjangkit dengan mudah penyakit ini. Mana-mana Raju, mana-mana Akmal, mana-mana Tiong, mana-mana Fadhli boleh terperosok.

Dalam kajian kami, tingkah laku lazim penyokong NVE termasuklah menyebarkan propaganda dalam talian, terlibat langsung dalam konten, komen atau ucapan kebencian, sebahagian dari penganjuran protes secara aman atau mengumpulkan dana untuk kumpulan radikal, tanpa terlibat dalam serangan fizikal secara langsung. Ada dalam kalangan mereka menjadi anggota atau pemimpin (misalnya ketua pemuda) organisasi tertentu yang berpegang atau berubah kepada NVE tanpa sedar ini.

Seperti rasuahisme, NVE sukar untuk dikekang kerana terdapat dilema kebebasan bersuara. Kita bergelut dengan dengan cabaran untuk mengimbangi antara keperluan keselamatan negara dengan hak terhadap kebebasan bersuara. Oleh sebab itu, keadaan ini menyulitkan tindakan terhadap individu yang memegang pandangan ekstrem ini, yang kadang-kala adalah sebahagian dari penggubal undang-undang atau agamawan, dan kelihatan seolah-olah tidak melakukan sebarang pelanggaran undang-undang.

Pengkaji NVE seperti kami sentiasa bimbang dengan gejala NVE takut-takut ia menular. Kami malah diburuk-burukkan dengan istilah baru, istilah ceplos dan diugut. Kerja kami adalah memantau ekstremisme tanpa kekerasan kerana retorik ekstrem sentiasa boleh menjadi titik permulaan kepada proses radikalisasi atau berfungsi sebagai persekitaran ideologi yang menyuburkan kemungkinan berlakunya tindakan ganas pada masa mendatang.

Oleh sebab itu kami akan sering diserang dan dianggap penentu atau 'kelompok terpaling' dalam menentukan apakah atau dimanakah batas antara perbezaan pendapat politik yang sah dengan proses radikalisasi yang berbahaya. Bahkan sebagai ahli sosiologi, kami menemukan kesukaran untuk menggerakkan perdebatan sihat yang penting dalam sistem perundangan dan dalam kalangan aktivis komuniti.

Bahaya yang saya sebutkan di atas boleh menjadi bah besar yang mengorbankan kemerdekaan negara kita sekiranya ia bergabung. Rasuahisme yang licik dan boleh bermutasi mampu bergabung dan bertindak sebagai ejen pemangkin kepada ekstremisme tanpa kekerasan. Ia boleh diwakili dalam format dua organisasi yang bekerjasama segenap tenaga sebagai satu barisan atau perikatan. Ia juga boleh bersenyawa dan bertindih beroleh cucu-cicit apabila mereka saling sokong-menyokong.
Mereka akan memperlihatkan hasrat mereka sebagai satu wawasan murni, menjenamakan diri sebagai pejuang, dan sangat cekap melakukannya.

Seperti yang saya sebut di awal, saya belum lihat usaha bersungguh-sungguh mana-mana pihak untuk meredam dan meredakan gejala ini. Dalam kalangan raja-raja Melayu, tuanku baginda yang aktif dan boleh diharapkan berperanan aktif melakukannya adalah pemerintah Perak iaitu Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah, dan Yang-di-Pertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan iaitu Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir. Baginda berdua boleh menggerakkan satu kempen besar menyelamatkan kemerdekaan negara ini bersama-sama baginda tuanku yang lain.

5fa996bb1317a29e: When governments impose economic sanctions, like the “economic D-Day” US president Donald Trump is now imposing on Iran, they portray them as a precision instrument—a scalpel rather than a sword—capable of pressuring ruling elites while sparing ordinary citizens.
This narrative has been used to justify some of the most sweeping acts of economic coercion in modern history. The only problem is that the central premise is untrue.

The case against sanctions is not merely strategic—that they rarely achieve their stated foreign-policy objectives—but also moral. Sanctions, particularly financial ones, do not fall equally on a population.

They fall hardest on those least able to bear them: low-income, wage-dependent, and publicly employed people. Thus, anyone who claims to care about the ethics of coercive statecraft must confront its distributional realities with the same rigour applied to questions of military tactics.

Cross-country research spanning decades has documented that economic sanctions reduce GDP growth, widen income inequality, increase child mortality, limit access to healthcare, and expand food insecurity in target states. These are not marginal effects.
One study found that US sanctions produced a poverty gap more than 3.8 percentage points larger in targeted countries than in comparable unsanctioned ones.
Another documented that UN sanctions reduced life expectancy by 1.2–1.4 years. These are statistics of mass harm, describing damage done to households, not palaces.
Yet the cross-country evidence, while damning, did not always tell us precisely who bears what burden within a sanctioned society.

In a new study using detailed microdata from Iranian household income and expenditure surveys and consumer-theoretic welfare metrics, we quantify the monetary welfare losses inflicted on Iranian households by the US-led 2012 SWIFT financial sanctions.
The 2012 sanctions severed all Iranian banks from the global payments system in the most comprehensive financial decoupling ever imposed on a major economy.

As a result, poorer Iranian households lost 2.3–2.8 times more, as a share of their pre-sanctions real (inflation-adjusted) expenditures, than higher-income households, and the average household lost 13%–42% of its pre-sanctions purchasing power.
Thus, financial sanctions reverse the distributional predictions typically associated with trade or commodity sanctions. They are not merely harmful but regressive.

The regressivity is not incidental. It reflects the mechanics of how financial sanctions function. When a country is cut off from the global payments system, it loses the ability to process international transactions, import intermediate goods, and maintain foreign-exchange reserves.
The immediate consequence is inflation, which disproportionately affects imported consumer goods and inputs that ordinary households depend on.

Since wealthier households tend to have more diversified assets, foreign-currency holdings, and access to informal financial channels, they can partly insulate themselves as poorer households absorb the price shock in full.
The sectoral impact is similarly unequal. Workers in manufacturing and services, which are deeply integrated into international supply chains and depend on imported inputs, suffer disproportionately.
Public-sector employees, whose salaries are denominated in a currency whose real value collapses as sanctions bite, also bear an outsize burden.

In the Iranian case, households headed by public-sector workers needed 35%–41% more compensation than their private-sector counterparts to maintain their pre-sanctions standard of living. Those employed in manufacturing and services required 37%–42% more than workers in agriculture and construction.

These are not abstractions. They represent real losses in nutrition, health, education, and dignity for millions of families who have no voice in the geopolitical disputes that triggered their impoverishment.

In the perverse political economy of sanctions, this popular suffering is justified as a means of pressuring the target government. But that rarely happens. Authoritarian regimes have proven remarkably adept at insulating themselves from the economic pain felt by marginalised populations.

After the 2012 sanctions, politically connected Iranians maintained real purchasing power while public-sector wage earners—teachers, nurses, civil servants—experienced a collapse in their living standards.
Some will argue that without sanctions, policymakers have no tool short of military force to impel a government to change its behaviour. But this, too, is false.

Diplomatic isolation, multilateral condemnations, targeted asset freezes, visa restrictions on ruling elites, and the patient construction of international mechanisms of legal accountability all carry far lower humanitarian costs.

The question is not whether states should have foreign-policy tools, but whether any tool that imposes the scale of civilian harm documented in the sanctions literature can be considered legitimate under the same ethical and legal frameworks we apply to armed conflict.
In wartime, the principle of proportionality limits permissible harm to civilians in pursuit of military objectives. Yet no equivalent principle governs economic coercion.

Sanctions are routinely imposed, tightened, and maintained for years or decades with little systematic accounting of their human costs. The civilian harm they inflict is treated as regrettable collateral damage rather than a direct moral consequence of the sanctioning state’s choices.

This inconsistency is indefensible. If it is impermissible to bomb a civilian water treatment plant, it should also be impermissible to sever a country from the global banking system when the foreseeable and documented effect is to deprive low-income families of one-third or more of their real income.

This is not an argument for passivity in the face of aggression or human-rights violations. But financial sanctions, as currently practiced, rarely achieve their strategic objectives, and they inflict predictable, severe, and regressive harm on civilian populations who bear no responsibility for the policies sanctions are meant to punish. Such harms are not more humane; they are harder to see and easier to ignore.
But policymakers now have the analytical tools to measure these harms precisely. What is still missing is the political will to take such measurements seriously.

That requires acknowledging that low-income people in Tehran, Caracas, Pyongyang, and Moscow are human beings whose welfare imposes obligations on those who would use their suffering as an instrument of geopolitical leverage.

Until sanctions regimes are held to the same humanitarian standards as military operations—with the same requirements to demonstrate proportionality, minimise civilian harm, and account for foreseeable consequences—their supposed ethical superiority to war will remain a convenient moral fiction for those who bear none of their costs.

83381e29250fd4f3: From Liew Li Xuan

Every August, Malaysians celebrate the country's independence, raise the Jalur Gemilang and revisit the story of a young nation beginning to determine its destiny. But perhaps the more important question is not what independence gave Malaysia, but what independence should now give Malaysians.

This year’s National Day theme offers an important clue. “Malaysia Madani: Kesejahteraan Dinikmati” suggests that it is not only "kesejahteraan" (wellbeing), but also "dinikmati" (experienced, enjoyed, felt) - that development should be judged not only by what a country produces, but by what its people are able to do with it.

Malaysia has made genuine progress. Our economy has expanded, infrastructure has transformed the country, education has become more accessible and millions of Malaysians have achieved a more secure standard of living.
These are important achievements. But they lead us to a larger question: what should prosperity ultimately enable a person to do?

A higher income matters. A cash transfer matters. A new highway matters. But none of these, by themselves, constitute a good life. A good life is the ability to make choices - being able to choose a career without being priced out of housing; start a family without viewing financial stability as unrealistic; retire without anxiety; remain in one’s hometown without sacrificing access to opportunity.
For a young Malaysian, it may simply mean being able to look at the country and believe: I can build my future here.
Perhaps Malaysia’s next phase of development should be less concerned with simply giving people more, and be more concerned with giving people greater capacity to build their own lives.
Public policy should not be measured only by how much the government spends, but by what people are eventually able to do without needing that intervention.

A cash transfer can help a family through a difficult month. But quality education can change the trajectory of a generation. A subsidy can reduce today’s burden, but a productive, well-paid job can reduce tomorrow’s dependence. Industrial investment can create employment, but a skilled workforce can create lasting mobility.
The ultimate goal of social protection should be greater independence, not permanent dependence.

That does not mean abandoning those who need support. A compassionate society must have a safety net. But a strong safety net should become a bridge — helping people through vulnerability while creating pathways towards greater security and self-reliance.

This is particularly important as Malaysia enters an era of rapid technological change. Artificial intelligence may create new industries and opportunities, but it could also widen inequalities if access to technology, education and reskilling remains uneven.

The same principle applies geographically. Malaysia’s success cannot be measured only by what happens in Kuala Lumpur, Penang or Johor’s industrial corridors. Development should give people the freedom to move if they want to, not force them to move because they have no other choice.

The generation that experienced Merdeka inherited a country still defining itself. The present generation inherited a country that has achieved sovereignty but faces a different challenge: making that sovereignty meaningful in everyday life.
For us, the fruits of independence lie in the freedom of a person to imagine a future and have a reasonable chance of reaching it.
The first generation of independent Malaysia asked: what kind of country can we build? The next generation should ask: what kind of life should that country make possible?

The answer should not be a Malaysia where everyone owns the same things, earns the same income or lives the same way. It should be a Malaysia where the circumstances of one’s birth do not determine the boundaries of one’s ambition.

Where prosperity is not measured only by how high the skyline rises, but by how far a child from an ordinary household can rise. Where a graduate can find meaningful work, a young couple can imagine owning a home, a parent can provide without constant anxiety, and a rural community can prosper without becoming a city.
Selamat Hari Merdeka. May our prosperity open doors, and may every Malaysian have the freedom to walk through them.
Liew Li Xuan is a youth advocate and an FMT reader.

ac156855d3ffd4ab: From Ameena Siddiqi
In 2018, Malaysia was outraged by the marriage of a 41-year-old Malaysian man to an 11-year-old Thai girl. He was a father of six. She had never attended school. She became his third wife.
The marriage was solemnised in southern Thailand without shariah court approval. The man was later fined RM1,800 for marrying and practising polygamy without permission.
The case prompted public outcry, with the government announcing plans to amend the law to raise the minimum marriage age for girls from 16 to 18.
Eight years later, Malaysia still has no uniform law establishing 18 as the minimum marriage age for everyone, without exception.

Now the issue has returned in another form. Perak is considering a RM500 first-marriage incentive for youths aged between 15 and 35. The proposed incentive, passed unanimously at a youth assembly, is expected to be brought to the Perak executive council for further discussion before being considered for the 2027 state budget.
The age range was reportedly adopted because the Youth Development and Sports Act 2007 defines “youth” as beginning at 15.
Somebody took a definition used for youth development and applied it to marriage. Did nobody stop to ask what it means to place a 15-year-old within a government marriage incentive?
Not a transferable definition

At 15, someone may be called a youth in sports, leadership or entrepreneurship. Under Section 2 of the Child Act 2001, that same person is a child. Marriage creates lifelong legal, emotional, physical and financial responsibilities. A definition suitable for one programme cannot be transferred to another without examining its possible harm.

I cannot imagine allowing my 14-year-old son to marry next year. He is still discovering who he is and beginning to understand relationships, consequences and responsibility. He should be thinking about school, friendships and his future.

I also think of a woman I once met who was married at 15. When I met her, she was 31 and raising seven children alone. She had studied only up to Form 3, had no career and did not know where her husband was.

The adults who allowed or encouraged that marriage may have believed they were solving immediate problems. But where were they when the marriage failed? Who ensured her children were properly cared for? Who was accountable when her husband disappeared? She and her children lived with the consequences.

I married at 19. Even then, I struggled with the responsibilities and pressures of marriage despite having family support. Marriage is difficult even for adults with education, employment and life experience. What makes us believe a 15-year-old is equipped to carry its burdens?
Is this ‘sakinah’, ‘mawaddah’, and ‘rahmah’?

In Islam, marriage is associated with “sakinah, mawaddah and rahmah”: tranquillity, love and mercy. (Surah al-Rum, verse 21). These ideals require maturity, compassion, responsibility and the capacity to understand and fulfil another person’s rights.

Can a marriage with a child realistically offer tranquillity, love and mercy when she may have to leave school, become financially dependent, experience early pregnancy and enter a relationship in which she has little power?
A marriage certificate cannot manufacture maturity, transform dependency into security or turn vulnerability into meaningful consent.
If adults are delaying marriage because of insecure work, low wages, unaffordable housing or expensive wedding expectations, address those problems. But do not draw children into that policy.
Where was the harm test?
Before adopting a law, policy, programme or budget decision affecting children, governments should examine its potential effect on their rights.

The Child Rights Impact Assessment asks which children may be affected and examines direct and indirect consequences for their education, health, safety, development and autonomy. It considers whether vulnerable groups will bear greater harm, whether children have been consulted, and whether the intended benefit can be achieved through a safer alternative.

Article 3 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child requires that “the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration” in actions undertaken by administrative authorities and legislative bodies.

Was any child rights impact assessment conducted before 15-year-olds were included in the Perak proposal? If so, where is it? How was a proposal affecting children unanimously approved without anyone first examining the possible harm?

Islamic jurisprudence offers a compelling test. The prophetic teaching “la darar wa la dirar” means, “There should be neither harm nor reciprocation of harm”. From it, Muslim jurists developed the legal maxim that harm must be removed. (Hadith 32, Forty Hadith of Imam al-Nawawi).
Good intentions are not enough. Those exercising authority must look beyond a proposal’s immediate benefit and examine the damage it could create.
What is the proposed benefit? RM500 to reduce the cost of beginning married life. What is the foreseeable harm?
A government appearing to legitimise marriage during childhood, with the risks of interrupted education, early pregnancy, financial dependence, isolation and abuse; Can RM500 outweigh that?
Protection cannot remain selective

Section 8 of the Islamic Family Law Enactment (Perak) 2004 sets the minimum marriage age at 18 for males and 16 for females, while permitting marriage below those ages with the written permission of a shariah judge.
However, a judge’s signature does not return a child to school, or remove the risks of pregnancy, dependency or abuse. It cannot give a minor the maturity or bargaining power of an adult.

A child is a child in Perak, Selangor, Kelantan, Sabah and Sarawak. Her protection should not depend on her gender, religion or postcode. How many more times must child marriage return before we end it?

Perak must remove everyone below 18 from the proposed incentive. Malaysia must set 18 as the minimum marriage age regardless of gender, religion or location. Remove the exceptions. Require child rights impact assessments for laws and policies affecting children. Publish the findings. Support vulnerable children and their families before marriage is ever considered.
We were outraged in 2018. We promised reform, but now we are still asking the same questions. The harm is foreseeable. The child is visible. The excuse is gone.
Ameena Siddiqi is the communications manager of SIS Forum (Malaysia).

d5dae1681de72f50: I’m not a fan of Bill Murray and I think “Groundhog Day” is even worse than “Lost in Translation” but in pre-Budget season we are all forced to endure the same old Groundhog Day debate about sales and services tax (SST) versus the goods and services tax (GST).

We know the script. Businesses say GST is better than SST. Of course they do. Everyone loves a tax they do not pay. I say a “black hair tax” is better than a “ginger hair tax” because I would not pay it. Businesses do not pay GST because they claim it back.
Former politicians tell us that GST is better than SST because it raises more government revenue. Of course it does. It is a tax on more goods and services paid by more people.
“Raising more revenue” means taking more money from the rakyat, especially the poor. This is why they are former politicians and fortunately will remain so.
Unfortunately, “tax experts” now tell us if only SST was more like GST, it would be more efficient. This is GST by the back door. They are fooling no-one except themselves.
We really need to stop the tax debates of the 1970s and drag ourselves, kicking and screaming, into the digital era of the 21st century.
I have said it before and I am going to keep saying it until someone listens, the best alternative to replace SST and GST is an electronic payments tax or EPT.

An EPT is a small charge on all electronic payments, for goods, services, fees and payments of every type, including pay-wave, credit and charge cards, debit cards and ATMs, e-money and e-wallets and normal bank payments and e-checking accounts online.
It is paid automatically at the point of the electronic transaction. Cash payments would be exempt.
The main advantage of an EPT is that it replaces complex income and consumption taxes with a tiny, automatic levy collected directly through the banking system.
This reduces compliance and administrative costs to almost zero. There are no tax filings for individuals and corporations because it is recorded through the electronic payment system.

The government collects revenue automatically from a small number of financial institutions rather than auditing millions of individual accounts and the costly bureaucracy required to manage traditional income and sales taxes is removed.

The EPT would have a very broad tax base of around 18.4 billion retail transactions annually according to the latest data and because a vast majority of economic value moves through electronic channels, a very low tax rate can generate massive public revenue.

My estimates last year were that a 1% EPT could raise RM28.8 billion and a 2% EPT could raise almost RM60 billion without anyone really noticing. It is so small that people do not change their behaviour, which is a key feature of tax efficiency and if you really object you can always pay in cash to avoid the tax.

It is inherently progressive because wealthier individuals and large corporations make a disproportionately high volume of financial transactions, meaning they naturally bear a larger share of the total tax burden despite the flat rate.
Tax evasion is virtually impossible because automated electronic trails make it significantly harder to hide income or bypass tax obligations.

For the government it provides unheard of fiscal stability and predictability with funds assessed, deducted and sent to the ministry of finance instantly at the exact moment a transaction settles. If they collect too much, then it’s SARA untuk Semua every month, except for those with ginger hair.
So please change the movie and let’s watch Ghostbusters!

139565e2a102ba33: The search for Malaysians reported missing after the devastating flash floods in Nepal is, first and foremost, a humanitarian emergency.
Families need information, while Malaysian officials must work through damaged infrastructure, disrupted communications and some of the world’s most difficult terrain in the world.
But beyond the immediate rescue effort, the disaster offers an important foreign-policy lesson. Malaysia needs strong relations with Nepal, China and India simultaneously.
Such relationships are not merely about trade agreements, investments, diplomatic visits or summit declarations.
When Malaysians encounter danger abroad, good bilateral relations can become practical channels for information, coordination and assistance.
The floods struck Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the frontier with Tibet. Geography therefore matters enormously.
The Himalayas may be divided by international borders, but rivers, mountain passes, transportation networks and natural disasters do not necessarily respect them.
Nepal is, naturally, Malaysia’s most important partner in locating missing Malaysians.
Nepalese authorities exercise sovereignty over the affected territory.

Their police, armed forces, disaster-management agencies, tourism authorities and local communities possess the knowledge necessary to determine where foreign travellers were last seen and where rescue operations should be concentrated.
This illustrates why diplomatic relations matter during emergencies.
Embassies are sometimes viewed as institutions primarily responsible for official visits, economic promotion and diplomatic protocol.
Yet when citizens disappear overseas, embassies become part of a country's emergency-response infrastructure.
Nepal, however, sits between two Asian giants.
To its north lies China.
The affected region is close to Tibet and the Nepal-China frontier.
China possesses significant transportation infrastructure, satellite capabilities, emergency-response resources and administrative networks across its side of the Himalayas.
Malaysia’s relationship with Beijing therefore cannot be measured solely through economics.
China has long been Malaysia’s largest trading partner. But mature bilateral relations should extend beyond exports, investments and industrial projects.

Strong government-to-government channels allow Kuala Lumpur to seek information and assistance whenever Malaysians encounter emergencies where Chinese capabilities or geographical proximity may prove valuable.
To Nepal’s south lies India. India possesses enormous logistical advantages in responding to emergencies in Nepal.
The two countries share a long and unusually open border. India’s armed forces and disaster-response agencies also possess extensive experience operating in Himalayan conditions.
Malaysia therefore needs an equally substantive relationship with New Delhi.
The Nepal disaster demonstrates the limitations of interpreting Asia solely through the prism of China-India competition.
Malaysia does not need to choose between Beijing and New Delhi.
Indeed, Malaysian interests are better served by maintaining strong relations with both.
During a Himalayan emergency, China can potentially contribute information, technology and logistical capabilities from the north.
India possesses substantial humanitarian and transportation capabilities from the south.
Nepal remains the sovereign state responsible for coordinating rescue operations within its territory.
Their capabilities can therefore be complementary rather than mutually exclusive.
This is why Malaysia’s foreign policy must remain pragmatic, independent and non-exclusive.
Strategic autonomy does not mean remaining distant from major powers. Neutrality does not mean indifference either.
It means maintaining sufficient diplomatic room to cooperate with different countries according to Malaysia’s interests and circumstances. The lesson extends to Asean.
Southeast Asia increasingly operates amid US-China competition, India’s rise and growing geopolitical fragmentation.
Smaller and middle powers face recurring pressure to align themselves with particular strategic camps.
Malaysia should resist unnecessary binary choices. Disasters demonstrate why.
Geography frequently demands cooperation precisely when geopolitics encourages separation.
Malaysia therefore needs diplomatic depth: a broad network of trusted relationships so that when one route, institution or communication channel fails, another can potentially be activated.
This becomes increasingly important as Malaysians travel, study, work and invest across the world.
Foreign policy, ultimately, is about people as much as power.
Malaysia needs Nepal because Malaysians travel there. Malaysia needs India because its geography and capabilities make it indispensable to South Asia.
Malaysia needs China because its economic weight, geographical position and strategic resources make it equally consequential.
Friendship with one should never require hostility towards another.
The Nepal tragedy therefore reinforces a longstanding Malaysian diplomatic instinct: cultivate many friendships while preserving strategic autonomy.
In peaceful times, these relationships generate trade, tourism, investment and diplomatic influence.
When catastrophe strikes, their value becomes far more fundamental.
They may help Malaysia bring its people home. May the force be with all.

b52e353415fcdf6e: Ministries can move fast if they want to. This was evident when the higher education ministry ordered an immediate halt to disciplinary proceedings against public university students over freedom of speech and public assembly issues on Aug 28.

The order came just two days after Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim asked to be given time to amend or repeal the Universities and University Colleges Act 1971 (Auku), arguing that comprehensive reform was needed to restore genuine student freedom.

Anwar told a student questioner at the Malaysia Madani Intellectual Forum Series 13 on the Nation’s Future Education and Auku at the Dewan Tunku Canselor, Universiti Malaya (UM): “I have fought this Act for a long time. Now we want to amend it comprehensively, so please give a little room.”
The student had asked for a guarantee that any new law replacing Auku would not simply be Auku in disguise. A fair question.

I wonder if Anwar, as he stood there, recalled that on Nov 10, 2014, those running UM had locked down the campus and refused to allow him to speak at this very same hall and that he was forced to stand under a streetlight on the campus grounds to address the gathered students.

I wonder if Anwar remembered that he was able to speak only because a bunch of students had defied the ban and forced open the university’s main gate at its Kuala Lumpur/Bangsar entrance and marched onto the campus, allowing him to step onto the grounds of his alma mater that night.
The university authorities called it trespassing and went after the students who had participated; but the students called it reclaiming their freedom.
Critics have long seen Auku as a relic of control, a tool to muzzle protests and political organising.
Auku stands as a monument to a specific philosophy of governance: that stability is best maintained by restricting the expression of dissent.
As prime minister, Anwar amended Auku in March 2024 to increase student autonomy. But it did not go far enough, and claims of interference from students, staff and critics have continued.
I noted a slight change in Anwar's words: An Aug 15 report said he had announced that Auku would be abolished outright but on Aug 26 he said it would either be amended or repealed.
We will have to wait and see whether the scepticism of that forum participant on Aug 26 was justified.

But if Auku is repealed, it will mark a turning point for Malaysia’s higher education. It will likely resurrect education’s original purpose: to liberate the mind so that the nation can flourish through the inventive genius of its people.

Reasonable people know that a mind fettered by fear cannot seek the truth, and a people trained only in obedience cannot build a just society. In the realm of ideas, silence is the enemy of progress. True innovation arises from the friction of diverse viewpoints, courage to challenge norms, and freedom to experiment.

How often have we heard that education should kindle a flame, not fill a vessel? When university students are forbidden to speak, organise, or question the status quo, their spirit is dimmed. They become vessels of information rather than inventors of solutions.

Anwar himself offers a living testament. I would think that a major reason Anwar is comfortable with the cadences of Shakespeare, the practicality and ethical fire of Thiruvalluvar, the philosophical depth of Confucius, and the historical sweep of Ibn Khaldun, is that he was encouraged to think and explore ideas during his student years.

If students are trained only to conform - as they are in secondary and tertiary education today - the nation will stagnate; if they are taught to think clearly, question deeply, and act responsibly, they will drive progress.

But such freedom should not only be given to students; academic staff should also be freed of shackles. Fearful or conformist academic staff will not drive progress, will not inspire students to think. It will only help produce the so called “kangkong professor”.

Academic staff who speak up, professors and lecturers who challenge government policies and decisions, should not be targeted for punishment or be seen as trouble-makers. They must be assured that their tenures, salaries and career progression will not be affected if they were to express views that run counter to that of the government or the university’s governing body.

Indubitably, unfettered freedom risks instability. If students want greater freedom, they must act responsibly; they must understand that running to protest over anything and everything they dislike, or damaging property, is not acting responsibly.
Auku's abolition must therefore be paired with training in clear thinking, rhetoric, intellectual integrity, ethical reasoning and a sense of responsibility.

Students must learn to weigh arguments, distinguish truth from falsehood, and recognise that freedom carries a duty to the common good. They must learn to rise above emotions tied to race and religion in seeking the truth and a common human destiny.
The true purpose of education is to teach people how to think clearly, to distinguish true from the false, and to understand the intertextuality of ideas.
Universities - and even secondary schools - should become sanctuaries of free inquiry, not prisons of the state; they should not be fortresses of the past but laboratories of the future.
I am reminded of the words of the late Dr Tan Chee Koon, who was known as Mr Opposition and continues to be highly regarded even today.

In March 1984, the government was proposing to place restrictions on the behavior of students studying overseas on scholarships because some of them were attacking the government vehemently and had even allegedly called for its overthrow and termed it “kafir”.
Some officials had likened criticism of the government to biting the hand that fed them.

Describing the idea that students should be grateful to the government as “feudal and outdated,” Tan said: “It is the duty of the Barisan Nasional government or of any other government to provide for the needs of our students or of any of its citizens.”
Students who were fortunate enough to be selected for a course overseas, he said, should thank God and Malaysian tax payers for providing the funds to send them abroad.
Tan added: “The government should not treat them like schoolchildren and expect them to behave like adults.”
What he said in 1984 still rings true today.

68917948ae4fb993: From Rozannah Jeffrey
The defamation suit filed against veteran journalist P Gunasegaram by businessman Mohamad Salim Fateh Din has quickly become a debate about more than the article at the centre of the case.

On one side, critics have described the action as a form of strategic litigation against public participation (SLAPP), warning that such suits could have a chilling effect on journalists writing about matters of public interest.
On the other, there is an equally straightforward argument: anyone who believes his reputation has been unfairly damaged has the right to seek redress through the courts.
Both principles can exist at the same time.
Journalists must be free to scrutinise matters involving public money, major infrastructure projects and questions of governance.
They are also entitled to draw conclusions and express opinions based on the information available to them, within the boundaries set by the law.
That freedom would mean little if journalists were expected to avoid every subject simply because someone powerful might object to what is written.
At the same time, press freedom does not remove the right of another person to challenge what has been published about him.
If Salim and MRCB believe Gunasegaram’s article conveyed a defamatory meaning, they are entitled to ask a court to determine whether that line was crossed.
That does not make the journalist guilty.
Nor does the filing of a lawsuit automatically mean the action is an attempt to silence journalism.
Those are precisely the questions that should now be tested through the legal process.
Gunasegaram should be given the opportunity to explain the basis of his writing and why he believes it falls within legitimate public-interest commentary.
Salim and MRCB should similarly be allowed to explain why they believe the article damaged their reputations and went beyond permissible criticism.
The danger is in turning the dispute into a public verdict before either side has fully made its case.
Those concerned about press freedom are entitled to raise those concerns. Those concerned about reputational rights are equally entitled to do so.
But once the dispute is before the court, there is little value in trying to determine the outcome through public pressure, political loyalties or social media sentiment.
The court exists precisely for disputes such as this: to examine the words used, the context in which they appeared, the evidence behind them and the legal defences available.
There will be plenty to discuss once a judgment is delivered.
Until then, the fairest position is a simple one — let Gunasegaram defend his journalism, let Salim and MRCB defend their names.
And let the court decide.

8a14bd6330e25558: From Kua Kia Soong

Every year, as Malaysia celebrates Merdeka, we are treated to a familiar spectacle: flags everywhere, patriotic songs, military parades, politicians proclaiming their love of the nation, and solemn speeches about the sacrifices of our forefathers.
But there is one conspicuous absence. Where is our Remembrance Day?

Why does Malaysia have no national day to remember and honour the Malaysians who died fighting the Japanese fascist occupation during World War II, and those who subsequently sacrificed their lives fighting British colonial rule?
Other countries understand that a nation cannot celebrate its independence without remembering those who paid the ultimate price for it.

Britain has Remembrance Day. France remembers the Resistance. Vietnam commemorates those who died in its struggle for independence. China remembers the victims and resistance fighters of the Japanese invasion.
Across the world, nations build monuments, hold ceremonies and teach their children about those who fought and died for freedom.
Malaysia, however, seems to have developed a remarkable capacity for celebrating Merdeka while forgetting the dead who made freedom possible.
Resisting fascist occupation

The Japanese occupation of Malaya from 1942 to 1945 was not merely an interruption between British colonial rule and Merdeka. It was a brutal period in which Malaysians of different communities suffered and resisted.

My family and friends in Batu Pahat suffered the same. Thousands were killed, imprisoned, tortured, starved or displaced. The Japanese occupation exposed the brutality of fascism and colonial militarism alike.

Malayan resistance movements fought the Japanese and drew support from people of different ethnic communities. There were also Malaysians who fought alongside British forces, including members of the Malayan Volunteer Forces and the Force 136 underground resistance. They did not all share the same political ideology.
They did not all dream of the same post-war Malaysia. But they shared something fundamental: they resisted fascist occupation.

Some died carrying rifles. Others died in prison camps. Others were executed. Many never returned to their families. Shouldn't their sacrifice belong to Malaysian history? Or have we decided that remembering them is politically inconvenient?
Independence from British colonialism

Then came the fight against colonialism. The irony becomes even greater after 1945. Once the Japanese were defeated, Britain returned to Malaya and attempted to restore colonial authority. The struggle for independence then entered another phase.

Yet the official narrative of Merdeka has often reduced this complicated history to a neat story: the British eventually handed over independence to Tunku Abdul Rahman and the Alliance in 1957, and Malaysia was born from a peaceful constitutional transition.

That story is profoundly incomplete. There were other Malaysians who fought colonial rule – through trade unions, political organisations, anti-colonial movements, student organisations, peasant struggles and armed resistance.
Some were imprisoned. Some were killed. Some spent years in detention without trial. Some died in the jungles.
Can a nation simply erase people from its history because their politics later became unacceptable? That is the uncomfortable question Malaysia has never adequately confronted.
The dead do not vote
Perhaps this is why remembrance is so politically difficult: the dead cannot vote.

They cannot contest elections. They cannot demand that politicians put up their photographs on Merdeka billboards. They cannot complain when their names disappear from school textbooks. They cannot ask why some historical figures are elevated into national heroes while others are condemned to oblivion.
But history should not be determined by who happens to be politically useful to the living.
A mature nation should be able to say, "We honour the sacrifice without necessarily endorsing every political belief of those who made it."
We can acknowledge British servicemen who died defending Malaya against the Japanese fascists while simultaneously recognising that Britain was a colonial power.
History is not a courtroom in which we must declare everyone either a saint or a villain. It is a record of human beings, their choices, their courage, their mistakes and their sacrifices.
A Malaysian Remembrance Day
This raises a more fundamental question: what exactly are we celebrating on Aug 31?
If Merdeka is simply the transfer of administrative power from one elite to another, then perhaps there is no need for remembrance.
But if Merdeka represents the Malaysian people's long struggle against fascism, colonialism, racism, exploitation and oppression, then the people who fought those battles are central to the story.
Merdeka should not be reduced to a date on the calendar. It should be a historical memory. And memory requires names. It requires graves, monuments, museums and it requires school lessons.
Above all, it requires the courage to remember even those whose politics make us uncomfortable.

Malaysia should therefore establish a national Remembrance Day for the Fallen in the Struggle Against Fascism and Colonialism. It could be observed annually around Merdeka, perhaps on Aug 31 itself, or on a separate day preceding Merdeka.

The day should remember all Malaysians and British servicemen who lost their lives resisting the Japanese occupation and those who subsequently sacrificed their lives in the struggle against British colonial rule.
Their names should be researched, documented and publicly commemorated regardless of ethnicity, political affiliation or historical controversy.

A national memorial could record the names of the fallen. Museums and archives could preserve their stories. Schools could teach the history of resistance from multiple perspectives rather than presenting a sanitised nationalist narrative.

And every year, our prime minister, Cabinet members, opposition leaders, veterans, civil society organisations and ordinary Malaysians could gather – not to celebrate a political party, but to bow their heads for those who never lived to see the Malaysia they fought for. That would make Merdeka mean something deeper.
A nation that forgets its dead is not truly free

There is something deeply strange about a country that spends millions each year celebrating patriotism but has never established a national tradition of remembering all those who died in the struggles that preceded independence.
We ask our children to wave the Jalur Gemilang. We punish those who happen to hang the flag upside down. We ask them to sing Negaraku. We tell them to be proud Malaysians.

But do we tell them who died so that they could grow up in a country called Malaysia? Do we tell them about the resistance fighters who faced Japanese fascism? Do we tell them about the anti-colonial activists who were imprisoned or killed? Do we tell them about the workers, peasants, students and ordinary people who challenged colonial power?
Or do we prefer a comfortable history in which independence arrived neatly packaged on Aug 31, 1957?
Merdeka without remembrance is patriotism without history. And patriotism without history is little more than flag-waving.
This Merdeka, perhaps instead of asking only, "How proud are you to be Malaysian?" we should ask a more difficult question: "Whom have we forgotten?"

Until Malaysia is prepared to remember all its dead – including those whose political beliefs make our present-day politicians uncomfortable – we have not learnt the most important lesson of independence:
Freedom is never given by history. It is won by people – and some of those people paid for it with their lives.
Kua Kia Soong is a former MP.

11b59ab06884c5a5: From Moaz Nair

The PAS leadership's assertion that "Islam is best equipped to resolve the problems of a plural society" frequently encounters challenges in being accepted and drawing the confidence of non-Muslim communities.
Minority groups tend to perceive this narrative as political rhetoric engineered to garner electoral support.

Fundamentally, non-Muslim scepticism towards PAS stems from divergent political ideologies, apprehensions regarding the safeguarding of constitutional rights, and the systemic implications of religion-based policies.

Although PAS has instituted inclusive structural mechanisms — most notably upgrading the non-Muslims supporters wing (DHPP) into an associate wing — a substantial discrepancy persists between the party’s official assurances and the empirical reality of its rhetoric and policy implementation.
Role of non-Muslims
From an organisational perspective, elevating DHPP to an official wing does not fundamentally alter the membership status of non-Muslims; they remain associate members rather than full members.
The party’s highest tiers of decision-making and policy formulation remain the exclusive purview of the syura council and the ulama council, bodies completely devoid of non-Muslim participation.
This hierarchical framework reinforces the perception that minority representation within PAS lacks substantive political efficacy.

Consequently, institutional initiatives and the establishment of auxiliary wings are frequently interpreted as cosmetic gestures or acts of electoral pragmatism, particularly when the leadership's practical actions fail to manifest genuine inclusivity.
'Supremacy' agenda

The PAS reliance on the narrative of "Malay-Muslim supremacy" and the agenda of solidarity of the ummah (Muslim community) to consolidate its core constituency has inadvertently alienated non-Malay communities.

Political discourse intersecting with racial and religious sensitivities — frequently deployed by factional leaders — has exacerbated social polarisation and undermined the sense of security among minority demographics.

Economically, doctrinally-rooted policies, such as the prohibition of gambling and restrictions on alcohol sales to uphold moral standards, have directly impacted the market viability of non-Muslim enterprises.

The implications of these regulatory interventions extend beyond market contraction within the affected sectors; they are also perceived as an encroachment on lifestyle liberties guaranteed under the civil legal framework.
Challenge to civil courts

The enforcement of civil-moral regulations in PAS-governed states such as Kelantan and Kedah, including the penalisation of non-Muslim traders for violating "modest" dress codes, demonstrates that Islamic moral norms are increasingly intersecting with the non-Muslim sphere.
This phenomenon raises systemic concerns regarding the preservation of cultural and personal freedoms for minority groups.

Furthermore, assurances that the proposed amendments to the Syariah Courts (Criminal Jurisdiction) Act (Bill 355) apply exclusively to Muslims have failed to assuage the deep-seated apprehensions of the non-Muslim community.

Critics anticipate that efforts to expand the jurisdiction of shariah courts, alongside the long-term agenda to implement Islamic criminal law, or hudud, could compromise the integrity of Malaysia's dual legal system.

Incremental theocratic legislative expansion is argued to possess the potential to reshape the architecture of the Federal Constitution, thereby challenging the primacy of civil courts as guardians of constitutional equality and equitable economic opportunities.
Polarising rhetoric

The party's governance model, which upholds the doctrine of absolute ulama leadership (a theocratic elite), introduces both theoretical and practical contradictions regarding how the principle of egalitarian representation can be realised within a pluralistic federal framework.

Although the party’s technocratic and mid-level factions attempt to project a moderate, governance-oriented image, polarising rhetoric from the top leadership, including the explicit association of non-Muslims with corruption and moral decay, perpetuates a profound trust deficit.
In conclusion, the non-Muslim electorate maintains a pragmatic "wait-and-see" posture.

Their assessment of PAS is not predicated on manifesto promises or superficial structural reforms; rather, it is measured empirically through state-level public policy outcomes and the rhetorical consistency of the party's elite.

80da8f6999ea9811: To say that the Elite Highway is congested is an understatement. Bursting at the seams is more like it. Anyone who regularly travels to KLIA Terminal 1 or 2 from Damansara, Elmina, Shah Alam, Subang Jaya and surrounding areas knows the frustration.

A journey that should take a reasonable amount of time can now easily stretch towards two hours, particularly during peak periods, weekends and festive seasons. And it is not just traffic heading to KLIA. Travelling in the opposite direction, coming from KLIA, can sometimes be even worse.
Perhaps the Elite highway should now be renamed the “Elite Turtleway”.
A 30-year gap
Built in the mid-1990s and completed in October 1997, the Expressway Lingkaran Tengah, or Elite, was a well-conceived project for its time.

It was designed primarily to provide a fast and direct connection to the then-new Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Sepang from the North-South Expressway, as well as from Shah Alam, Subang Jaya and the western Klang Valley.
But that was almost 30 years ago, when Elite had only seven interchanges.

Since then, the Klang Valley and southern Selangor have been transformed. Putrajaya, Cyberjaya, Dengkil, Bandar Saujana Putra, Gamuda Cove, Serenia City, Nilai and numerous new townships and industrial areas have emerged.
Practically every major highway in southern Selangor is now connected, directly or indirectly, to Elite.
Five additional interchanges have since been added, bringing the total to 12, along this 60km corridor between Shah Alam and Nilai, with the link to KLIA now but a secondary spur.
This raises an uncomfortable question.

Did PLUS management trade our future congestion nightmares for more interchanges? And consequently generating more highway access fee payments from developers and more toll revenue from the additional traffic generated?
There is nothing wrong with providing access to new developments. Developers need connectivity and concessionaires have legitimate commercial interests.
But there is another side to the equation. Who considered the cumulative impact of all these additional connections on the capacity of Elite itself?

The really important question, however, is not whether PLUS earned additional revenue. It is whether the concessionaire and the authorities properly accounted for the cumulative traffic impact of each new interchange.
Every new interchange may make economic and development sense for the surrounding area. But every new connection also potentially feeds more vehicles onto the same highway with the same capacity.
At what point do we stop asking how to connect more developments to Elite and start asking whether Elite can still cope with all the traffic we are putting onto it? That is the real issue.
Elite today is no longer simply an airport link. It has become a major regional distributor carrying traffic from a much wider area. And therein lies the problem.

We have continued to add development, new townships, industrial areas, interchanges and connecting highways, but we are not making it any easier for us to move. Our mobility is becoming more restricted and we are spending more time on the roads travelling over much shorter distances. In one sentence, we are creating our own mobility trap.
By right, the more we progress the more mobile we should become, and moving over shorter distances, like going to the airport, should be quick and easy, like a walk in the park.
Additional pressure from KLIA
KLIA, the main reason Elite was built, is generating and attracting substantially more traffic now due to its phenomenal growth after the pandemic.
In 2025, KLIA handled about 63.3 million passengers, with Terminal 1 alone handling 32.1 million - well above its original 25-million-passenger design capacity.
Terminal 2, which handled slightly less traffic is expected to overtake Terminal 1 in passenger numbers soon as the annual growth of passenger traffic among the low cost airlines is much higher.
More passengers inevitably mean more cars, taxis, e-hailing vehicles, buses, airport workers, logistics vehicles and other traffic accessing the airport.

So the question we should also be asking is: does the entire ground transport network, including Elite, have sufficient capacity to serve KLIA - today and into the future? Increasingly, the answer is no.

Had Elite remained primarily an airport access corridor, perhaps the current congestion would not have reached this level. But it has progressively taken on a much wider role without a corresponding expansion of capacity and alternative routes.
MEX 2: the missing alternative

The stalled MEX 2 project is also part of this story. It was planned to provide a more direct connection from the MEX 1 Putrajaya interchange to KLIA, giving motorists another route to the airport and reducing dependence on Elite.

Its failure to materialise means that traffic which could potentially have been distributed through another corridor continues to depend heavily on Elite. But completing another highway alone will not solve Elite's long-term problem.
What we need is forward network planning and proper traffic distribution, involving not only roads but also rail and other forms of dedicated public transport.
For instance, why can't a rail line be built to connect coastal Selangor with KLIA?

In essence, an urgent, comprehensive study is needed to determine the current and future travel demand to and through Elite, identify the demand's origin, and determine how it should be distributed across the road and rail network.

The objective should not simply be to build more roads to accommodate more cars. The objective should be to build a transport network with sufficient capacity, resilience and alternatives - one that improves our overall mobility index and makes travelling to KLIA a smooth and predictable journey, rather than a stressful race against time.
One thing is certain: we cannot continue to assume that infrastructure built for the traffic demands of the last century will remain adequate for the needs of the 21st century.
Elite has served us well for almost 30 years. But the question now is whether we are prepared to redesign the network around the realities of today - and the demands of tomorrow.

10b5d54c0f2a0d92: At my local government clinic recently, I sat among many fellow Malaysians, feeling at peace with things. That I was there meant I’m still alive, and whatever ailment afflicts me is not fatal. Not immediately so anyway.

Lately, my presence at such clinics has become more frequent. But I'm not quite a leach on our national health service, mind you. I still have my own private medical insurance. For more serious issues, I still go to see specialists at private hospitals and help them buy their second Ferrari.

I’m as old as our nation. But while nations can be full of vim and vigour even after decades and centuries of existence, the human body is more frail. We mere mortals each have an expiry date and each passing day takes us one day closer to that date.

Enough of doom and gloom. At such clinics I get to see the real Malaysia in all its glory and all its frailties. The geography of Malaysia is no doubt amazing, as is our food and culture, but people are what make the country what it is.

Malaysians have our own history of acrimony and angry discourse, at times teetering towards being a failed nation. But, and this is an important but, we haven’t gone over it yet, while many other countries have. Long may it remain that way.

If you’re in a Malay or Chinese or Indian neighbourhood, that’s what you get – a Malay or Chinese or Indian microcosm of the nation, splendid by itself, but not quite a full representation of the soul of Malaysia
Unfortunately, you won’t see very much of it elsewhere either, whether at government schools, the civil service, corporate offices or gated neighbourhoods and condominium apartments.
Separate but together

Malaysia has become very compartmentalised. We’re not actually hostile to each other, apart from the usual rabble-rousers garbed in the flags of political parties or robes of religions. But we’re not very close either. We seem to meet and deal with others at the edges and peripheries of our ethnic comfort zones.

I'm certainly not trying to make the case that being at a government health clinic is a great unifying experience. While I elect to be there, there are many who don’t have that option, and the burden of illnesses or injuries they carry can often be seen in their faces and bodies.

Let me rattle off the positives for me, though. First, this is our tax ringgit at work, doing what tax ringgit is supposed to do. Unfortunately, vast amounts of our tax ringgit is regularly siphoned away to enrich some unprincipled fellow citizens feasting on our shared wealth.

Second, those at the clinic have more important things weighing on their minds than just observing their fellow Malaysians. They could be in need of medical treatment, or they could be the carers of such people. Unlike me, I doubt if many would actually say they enjoy being there.

I like their honesty and lack of pretension and entitlement. Nobody cares very much about who you are outside of the clinic. If we talk at all, it’s often just to ask about or explain the unfortunate circumstances that brought us there.

How often do we see fellow Malaysians of all backgrounds seated together side by side without looking uncomfortable? Most of our public places, especially ones that require us to be close with each other – restaurants, food courts, places of worship - seem to be divided almost exclusively by ethnicity.
See the good in ourselves

Third, the clinic staff appear to be hardworking and dedicated, in spite of their workload in handling a constantly increasing number of patients. I wouldn’t smear them with the usual generalisation of lazy public servants. Any capitalist would’ve been more than happy to have these people in their employ.

When we whinge about Malaysia, and God knows there are enough reasons for us to do so, we often fail to realise there’s that abstract entity called Malaysia and there are real flesh and blood Malaysians.

There isn’t much most of us can do to change the nation, regardless of our desire and wishes. There are powerful forces – fear, greed, insecurity – lined up against us. Often, these forces win and even change us into what we started out hating.

Most of us have been driven apart by so much divisive rhetoric and acts, especially political ones, that we seek comfort only among our kind, at most giving polite smiles and spouting empty words about diversity and fairness and unity.
Change from within

But there’s a lot we can do to help ourselves and our fellow Malaysians regardless of the usual divisive factors, as opposed to trying to change the entire nation. Changing how we see and treat each other is well within our control. The usual barriers of language, religions, culture etc are mostly in our minds, and can be overcome.
Let the politicians worry about getting millions of votes. Let us instead worry about changing the minds of those in our immediate circles of family, friends, neighbours, colleagues.

Let us remind each other that while Malaysia has its fair share of bad leaders, most Malaysians are just like us. In spite of our differences, we should be united by what we have in common: that we want to lead a good life and do the best we can for those we love.

A government medical clinic is a great place to see these things we have in common. We all grow old, often get sick and need to have the care and attention of our fellow Malaysians. At some point this becomes so important that we forget about anything else.
The universe has a way of showing us we’re all the same underneath our differently-coloured skin. We should realise this earlier rather than later, so that we can still do something about it.
To my fellow Malaysians, I wish you good health, long life and Merdeka, Merdeka, Merdeka!

c3655063932d8091: US president Donald Trump has once again expressed his interest in meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un. But Kim’s sister, who is one of his closest advisers, has already poured cold water on the idea.
Whether this is a sign of disinterest or a bargaining tactic, two questions immediately arise: Where does Trump expect any talks with Kim to go? And how does he intend to achieve his objective(s)?

The goal of Trump’s conversations with Kim during his first presidency was to bring about North Korea’s nuclear disarmament. He failed. Since then, North Korea’s warheads have increased markedly (to 57, says Trump), as has the range and accuracy of missiles that could deliver them throughout the region and around the world.
The same effort now is all but guaranteed to have the same result. Kim almost certainly believes his security rests on having a credible nuclear deterrent.

Kim has no doubt noted that the US attacked an Iran that did not have nuclear weapons, that it did the same with Iraq, and that Nato did the same with Libya after its leadership surrendered its nuclear programme.
Likewise, Russia invaded Ukraine in 2014 and again in 2022, after Ukraine gave up its post-Soviet nuclear arsenal in exchange for security assurances that were not honoured.

Kim also understands that there would be little interest in him if North Korea did not possess nuclear weapons. His and the country’s relevance and international standing depend in no small part on a growing stockpile.
Trump exaggerates two factors underlying his confidence that diplomacy will pay off. The first is the lure of personal diplomacy.

Virtually every American president believes that his powers of persuasion and personal relationship with any given foreign leader matter a great deal. History suggests the opposite is closer to the truth.

Trump also appears to exaggerate the lure of economic development that could benefit North Korea if international sanctions are lifted. What matters most to Kim is his continued rule and the rule of his chosen successor, rather than the prosperity and happiness of North Koreans.
If anything, opening up the country could threaten his grip on power. Revolutions are more likely to come about amid rising expectations than under effective repression.

So, if disarmament is not a realistic goal, it is possible that some version of arms control is. Establishing limits on the quantity and quality of North Korea’s nuclear and missile forces could be worth exploring.

It comes at some risk, though, as it would be seen as legitimising and accepting North Korea’s decision to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and build a weapons programme, leaving many in South Korea and Japan uneasy or worse.

North Korea’s support for Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine is also worth raising, although Kim is unlikely to stop providing such support given the energy and nuclear weapons-related assistance his regime reportedly receives in return. Here, too, there is a real question about what diplomacy might achieve, and at what cost.

That brings us to South Korea, a critical, long-term ally of the US. The Korean Peninsula was the venue of the first hot conflict of the Cold War. More than 36,000 Americans lost their lives, initially in liberating South Korea, and subsequently in a failed effort to unify the country by force.
South Korea today is a major success story, a case study in transformation from corrupt authoritarianism and dire poverty to vigorous democracy and a thriving economy, now the world’s 14th largest.

Trump appears to treat the relationship as zero-sum: that he is more likely to achieve his goals with North Korea if he sacrifices the US's relationship with South Korea. The opposite is more likely to be the case.

But history is not stopping Trump. He has imposed tariffs on South Korea despite a free-trade agreement, withdrawn missile defenses in the face of a growing North Korean missile threat, and, most recently, downsized and curtailed a major US-South Korean military exercise that he viewed as costly and unnecessarily provocative.
It is not clear what is motivating Trump. He may see in North Korea an opportunity for a foreign-policy success to distract from his failure in Iran.
Or he may simply be acting in a fit of pique over South Korea’s refusal to help him in a war it opposes (and which has meant higher energy prices and shortages of key manufacturing inputs).

What is clear is that Trump seems not to appreciate that deterrence depends on the ability to mount a credible defense. This is dangerous, not least because 28,000 US troops are stationed in South Korea, which the US is obliged by treaty to defend.

Trump’s diplomatic foray will fail if success is defined as persuading Kim to give up his nuclear weapons. Moreover, the diplomacy’s substance and form—conducted unilaterally, taking the South Korean government by surprise—is likely over time to undermine the credibility of US security guarantees.
Rather than one Korea with nuclear weapons, we could well find ourselves with two, increasing the prospect of war on the peninsula after three-quarters of a century.

Worse, the conditions that gave rise to nuclear stability during the Cold War will be extremely difficult to replicate, raising the specter of a nuclear weapon being used for the first time since 1945.
Richard Haass, president emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations, is a senior counselor at Centerview Partners and distinguished university scholar at New York University.
